Loren Schoenberg
Loren Schoenberg has distinguished himself in the jazz world as a tenor saxophonist, band leader, jazz educator, and Director of the Jazz Museum of Harlem.
He was interviewed in New York City on January 14, 2019 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive. I’m very pleased to have Loren Schoenberg here today. And I read through your resume, it only took a half an hour.
Bu-dump-bump.

Bu-dump-bump is right. But all the things you’ve done, I don’t like to bring myself into this but I can personally relate to cause I’ve done a few of them and I know they have required different talents. You started out playing the piano, right? Did you have a point in your teens where you said to yourself dammit, I’m going to be a musician. I’m going to make a living as a musician?

Well I don’t know how to say it. It was almost like pre-ordained or natural for me that this happened. I’m the youngest of three children and sometimes I think the youngest child they say is spoiled or has more options because maybe the parents had other experiences with the older children or something like that. So I evinced a talent for music early on, not a great talent but just I loved to play and I was always playing. And my high school band director had been a music theory major at Manhattan School of Music. And I really kind of cottoned to music theory, for whatever reason, and maybe because he was a great teacher in high school, and we had music theory. This was a normal high school, this was not an arts school, it was just Fairlawn High School in Bergen County, New Jersey, and somehow the career that my band director had had of becoming a music theory major, he had gone to Manhattan School of Music, somehow I kind of fell into that, that that was going to become my goal. And then there were no jazz degrees in those days, not really jazz programs so to speak. Juilliard had no jazz whatsoever, and Manhattan School of Music did have a good jazz band led by Rusty Dedrick, and a good faculty, and so I wound up being accepted to Manhattan School of Music. I guess we’re jumping ahead a little bit here. But I wound up being accepted there in 1976 as a theory major and piano minor. But the funny thing was that my parents, you know my parents were very supportive. I never even contemplated doing anything else. And they let me do that. It wasn’t as though well, like a lot of, I mean there was a kid lived down the street from me, Harry Ballan, much more talented than I am, played Brahms and played the © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
wonderful piano, and he was a year younger than me, than I. And so but his parents made him get a law degree. And I think that was probably how it was for most kids, but it wasn’t like that for me.
Yeah. They want you to have the, even if you go into music some of them want you to have the fall-back-on.
Right.
Right? Get that teaching degree or whatever.
Right. So that was a real leap of faith on my parents I guess. I was very lucky with my parents, which I can tell you more about.
Did you — were you turned on by the Swing Era music, and then the jazz that was being played at the time?

No. It’s all because of my father had a 78, a Decca 78 album of “The Jolson Story” with two pictures of white gloves on the cover. No picture of Jolson or anything like that. And I fell in love with his voice and phrasing. Now I was a strange kid, I mean I’m four years old and this is 1962 and I loved these records. And I used to imitate them, it was kind of strange for a little kid. And that got me into, I mean I was already kind of like — you know I should tie up the Jolson thread just for a moment, that the whole thing about minstrelsy and African-American culture actually wound up getting a head start, my being attracted to Al Jolson and then eventually having to come to terms with minstrelsy in general and Jolson in specific, who’s gotten a very rough deal. He’s become kind of like the straw man for talking about minstrels. It was just very unfair to him. But so unwittingly I was set into something that was going to force me to confront, you know, the overwhelming issue of America and that’s as W.E.B. DuBois put it so many years ago, race. So that pretty much everything I’ve done in my life has been somehow, in some sense been connected with those questions. But I went from there, I was a collector. I used to write NASA and get things about Gemini VI and Gemini, the little home film of the docking and all this kind of stuff. So I was that kind of kid who wanted to write letters and wanted to research things, for whatever, and then, because I wanted to see Al Jolson and then eventually I wanted to see old movies and I wanted to see old Warner Brothers films that were at theaters in New York City like the Theater 80 St. Marks and others, this would be the early 70s, that were showing old movies. And my parents, God Bless them, would bring me in from the suburbs and watch these old movies, which they weren’t particularly interested in. They had seen them when they came out and they weren’t at all interested in nostalgia or anything like that. And then I started seeing Ruby Keeler and Dick Powell and those movies and I kind of loved that stuff. And I was already going buying records and records in the local public library. And then eventually lucked upon Hollywood Hotel, which had Benny Goodman’s band in it. And then all of a © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

sudden I got this bug about oh boy, well all that other stuff was great but boy there’s something about that that really gets me. Well my local public library had a copy of Benny Goodman’s 1938 Carnegie Hall concert, a double LP, which influenced so many people of a certain age. And I fell in love with it. And I just loved listening to it. And at that point I had been taking — I started piano lessons when I was 4. And you know, a typical thing, an old lady who lived on my little street who had like a living room with heavy drapes — I mean it was your typical whatever that experience was you know. You felt like everyone was looking at you and you sat there and you played in the dark drapes and the old lady and the whole thing. But it worked well, you know what I mean? Not interested in jazz at all or anything like that, but I learned basic the Hanon whatever the heck it was.
The Hanon exercises.

Right. And John Thompson, “A Day in Bermuda” or whatever they called it. “A snowy Bird” you know, and learned all that stuff. And then, on this Benny Goodman record I listened to it and I looked at all the names and then in my local newspaper, the Bergen Evening Record I saw, I was about, I don’t know, 13 or 14, and it said, “Sundays at the Colonial Post on Main Street in Hackensack, New Jersey, Sundays maybe 5 PM to 8 PM Teddy Wilson.” And I said this cannot be the Teddy Wilson who’s on the Benny Goodman record I’m listening to at Carnegie Hall. I mean what would he be doing playing at an Italian restaurant in Hackensack, New Jersey? Well it turns out that Teddy lived in New Jersey as did Hank Jones, in Bergen County, and when he was around he took whatever gigs he could get just to keep his fingers in shape and maybe he was in between tours or whatever. And so my parents took me to see him and he was very kind and let me sit by the piano and look and all this kind of stuff. I mean I really had no inkling of what I was getting. I mean I knew he was great but all I knew was this one record and that I loved the music. And so my parents got to meet him. And that started a series of things where my parents would meet these musicians, now let’s put it in context. I mean these are African-American musicians. I’m a kid growing up in the 60s and 70s in Bergen County, New Jersey, which was one of the most un-diverse places there could be, although my town, called Fairlawn, was kind of unusual because it had a large Jewish population. On the day that my parents moved in in the 1950s to welcome the first Jewish family on the block everyone put up For Sale signs on all the houses, so they saw that as they drove up the first day. Then they took the signs down. So you know it was not a very diverse place. So what happened was my parents met Teddy Wilson and eventually met Hank Jones and eventually met Eddie Durham and a few other people who were so avuncular and so warm and supportive, my parents said we have no problem at all with our kid leaving him in these hands. Now if you had said to my parents your son’s going © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

to be a jazz musician and he’s going to be hanging out with these people with all the prejudices about, forget race for a moment, just about how jazz musicians are. I mean my parents were just normal, when I say normal people what I mean is they didn’t know anything about show biz or musicians.
He’s going to work in bars and live the night life.

Well, and all the negative connotations that again, due to race, that came to, you know as we find out that more, you know, physicians have problems with drugs than musicians, and that you know musicians are actually way down on the line. But anyway so you asked earlier about like when I knew I was going to be a musician — I think all these experiences kind of led to them. My parents saw like oh wow, there’s these wonderful mentors out there and they’re willing to answer Loren’s questions or something like that. And so that’s kind of part of the context.
That’s terrific.
Thanks.
You mentioned minstrel-y, you know, the minstrel practice.
Minstrelsy.
Minstrelsy, thank you.
Right. Still very prevalent in 2019. It is.
This is a hard — maybe a hard or way too simplistic question. But you teach jazz history, do you think that the development of the music has more to do with sociology or to do with musicology?
Oh sociology, hands down.
Okay.

Because I mean, I’m a college dropout so let’s get that straight. So I don’t know a lot of terms to be conversant with necessarily, and I might be confusing some that someone with an academic background might hear me talking and right now they’re rolling their eyes. But what I mean is that — well you mentioned teaching jazz history. We don’t get to Jelly Roll Morton or Sidney Bechet for a couple of months. So you know it’s all about New Orleans and English and French mercantilism, and what it was like to be colonized by the French or by the English or by the Spanish, and about of course New Orleans and about the great lives of the nineteenth century and about Gottschalk, Louis Moreau Gottschalk, and about Abe Lincoln and, all these things, and without laying a strong predicate or whatever the right word would be for that, then I don’t think you can really start to understand, I should say not you of course but a young student of 2019 who may not be enmeshed in history like earlier generations were, that it’s necessary to create this context. And then maybe we can start to understand who Armstrong was and who Bechet was and who Benny Goodman was and all these things. So about minstrelsy, I learned a © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

lot from reading Albert Murray and then getting to know him and Stanley Crouch and others, and just doing a lot of reading and talking to people, including musicians of the much older generations. I mean I got to know Zutty Singleton’s wife pretty well, which I’ll talk about when we talk about the New York Jazz Museum, and trying to put it all together in some way that makes sense. So I don’t know if that answered your question.
It did. Okay. You just returned from the Jazz Ed conference?
Jazz Education something.
Yeah. Jazz network thing, in Reno.
Yeah it was great.

Now when you’re out there and being surrounded with all those people and activity you might get one feeling about the state of jazz. When you come back here and you live here and you participate and you observe the jazz scene, do you get a different take on today’s state of jazz?

Well I wouldn’t say I get two different ones, they’re all part of one. It’s like not mirror images but it’s so inspiring going to those jazz conventions. I mean it’s just wonderful because you see what the music means to so many people who don’t live in New York or don’t live near the major metropolitan areas where there are jazz clubs. And these are the people that are keeping the flame alive in everywhere else in the country. And to see how the kids are so excited and all this kind of stuff, and they’re going to play their tune and they’re going to do this and they’re going to do that without realizing, and this kind of merges a little bit with your previous question, merging with American history. Every time you pick up an instrument to play jazz or to contemplate it, you’re part of some tradition, you’re following in footsteps, you know, defined by African-American geniuses. And you’re part of the story and it’s a great heritage. And it’s a heritage that you know is participated in by something that is for most of the time, fun, and playing an instrument and tapping your foot, and so it’s kind of profound. I mean it’s easy to look at jazz education or things like that less than charitably sometimes, when you realize that a large percentage of people who teach that never played in a band or never really had experience, I don’t find that very satisfying at the end of the day as not the proper way, but it’s how I look at it. I look at it, it’s all good. This is wonderful. These are people that love the music, we’ve got to support them and get to them however we can get to them. And a big problem with teaching, as I’m sure you know and we all know or as parents know, I’m not a parent, but that you can’t teach kids in 2019 assuming that they are like we were in 1976 or 1986 or as your students were in ’96 or ’06. It doesn’t work. And so consequently you know you’ve got to learn to adapt. And so that’s how I come back from the JEN convention in Reno, I heard some great music, I met some wonderful teachers, I met old friends, I made new friends, and I was just really pumped up just to see all these © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
people loving it. And I come back to New York and of course I’m very involved with the Jazz Museum and keeping an institution alive, and so yeah, it’s all part of one big picture.
It’s all good.

I don’t have a summation kind of thing, but I’m just again going back to something I wanted to say was I’m probably the luckiest person. You know some people say well there’s luck but there’s also this and that and being in the position to have luck or something like that. Nonetheless I am among the luckiest people that you’re ever going to interview.

All right. I consider myself pretty lucky too. And at one point I had had, because I was in the right place at the right time I got to ride to a gig with the Statesmen of Jazz, and like Milt Hinton was on my left, and he fell asleep on my shoulder. And I’m thinking, this is Milt Hinton and I’m with him, and Panama Francis and Claude Williams, and I’m just like, said to myself, you should really take note of this and appreciate it. So I’m wondering if you had that same feeling. You played beside, you know, Eddie Durham and Panama I mentioned and Russell Procope and — were you aware of the significance of that I guess it is if I have a question.

To the degree that a 19-year-old can, or a 25-year-old. Yeah. I mean if you want to work biographically up to how all those things happened, so I’m back in New Jersey, you know, and I’m a teenager, and my parents are meeting some of these people and I’m hearing Teddy Wilson and then Hank Jones also was playing solo piano at a place called the Sherry Netherlands and I used to go there. My parents would leave me and Hank would drive me home. Was I appreciating it as to what it really was? How could I? I was 16 years old. I knew that this was a great man and that I was very lucky to be around him. Now I look back at it and I’m like Jesus. But what happened was there was something in New York called the New York Jazz Museum. How I learned about it I don’t remember except I would have read about it in the paper. This was 1972. So I was 14, or turning 14 that summer. And I don’t know how it happened. I guess I read about it. I asked my parents to take me in. They took me in and I wanted to volunteer. And I wound up becoming a volunteer at this place as it opened. It was on West 55th Street between 6th and 7th, right just east of the City Center. And it was in an old carriage house that had been owned by the Rockefellers many, many years before. And there was a woman named Evelyn Cunningham who was a real figure in New York civil rights history, who worked for Nelson Rockefeller. And somehow between her and some other people they arranged for this to become a jazz museum. It was a long, it’s kind of like the shape of our place up in Harlem now, kind of a long, rectangular space. Not that big but it went back pretty deep. And the man ran it named Jack Bradley. And Jack, this was now 1972. Louis Armstrong died in ’71. Jack was a photographer and a guy who knew all — he was good © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

friends with Bobby Hackett and he was like an adopted son of Louis’s, of Louis Armstrong, and a lifelong disciple of his. And he wound up becoming the manager of this small little jazz museum. And he took me on as a volunteer. So every Saturday and Sunday I would take the bus — you could take a bus from suburban New Jersey into New York, it was easy, and my parents let me do it, unbelievable. And I wound up volunteering there for years. And this is where I got to know Marge Singleton, Zutty Singleton’s wife, it’s where I got to know Clarence Armstrong, who was Louis Armstrong’s, I guess he was a cousin, he was mentally challenged. In those days they used the word slow or retarded. I don’t know what the right term is. But he was kind of like a big child. And because Jack was so close with Louis and the family he would spend weekends there. A little bit later Duke Ellington was — we didn’t know but he was dying in the hospital so Harry Carney came in, and Harold Ashby used to come in and spend weekends just hanging around this jazz museum, so I got to know all these people. There was an opening of an exhibit on Count Basie and I brought my little — at that time I had a hand-held cassette machine that was about this big, you remember, that you press the button like this, and I remember bringing it in and I tape recorded on a cassette the first opening night. And it was Eddie Durham, Buddy Tate, Al Gray, Chuck Folds on piano, Eddie Jones on bass and Jo Jones on drums, and a few others who I got to know later. And Paul Quinichette was there. And then, who comes in but Basie. So Basie plays the piano. Then who muscles his way through the crowd — now Eddie Jones if you remember, I think you interviewed him.
Not the bassist.

Not the bassist. Eddie Jones was about six feet — he could have been a football player — like six foot six, big guy. Somebody comes and taps him on the shoulder and takes the bass. It’s Charles Mingus. And I recorded this on my little tape. I gave it to Phil Schaap, I never saw it again, but I’m just joking because Phil gave it back to me thirty years later.
Okay.

But anyway, but, so I was around these things. With the Jazz Museum, in the back they had a projection room where we would show films every Saturday or Sunday afternoon and my job as a 14 or 15-year-old was to actually thread them, you know the old fashioned thing, thread the movie into the camera and show it, and we would show “The Sound of Jazz” and we would show “Jammin’ the Blues.” So I saw these things, I don’t know, a hundred times or more by the time I was 15 or 16. I had many, many experiences at the Jazz Museum. Jack Bradley at that time was really kind of — and I met Dan Morgenstern at that time because Dan was on the board of the Jazz Museum. And we joke about it now because we’ve been friends for, you know, almost 50 years, which is that — I’m 60 now so that would have been 47 years ago but that he remembered me as a © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

kid just pestering him all the time you know. And so I met him there. And then we had an exhibit on Benny Goodman. And I was a Benny Goodman fanatic already based on having that record at the public library, and I had started corresponding with D. Russ Conner. We called him Russ Conner. Russ Conner was the guy who wrote BG on the Record, which is the first, excuse me, was the first biodiscography. Again it sounds like something you go to the doctor for.
Yeah, they treat you for that.

But that was a combination of a biography and a discography. And he had a book out called BG on the Record Benny Goodman on the Record. And I found it in a local library and I started writing him post cards about like where can I find the alternate take of “House Hop” or something like this. Because in those days it was hard to find, I mean there’s no internet, there’s no nothing in the record stores and all this kind of stuff, and so I was very much enmeshed in collecting and getting to meet the musicians who had worked with Goodman. Well when we were preparing for the Goodman exhibit, Hymie Shertzer came in and Hymie had been the lead alto player in Benny Goodman’s band back in the 30s. And he really couldn’t believe that like some kid knew who he was. And someone else came into the Jazz Museum, and I can’t remember his name but he was on WBAI radio, here in New York, a Pacifica station. And they did really kind of like esoteric programming and very leftish at that time. And somehow he said would you like — it was kind of weird to find this 14, 15-year-old kid that wants to hear this old music. I came on his radio show just to talk about the Jazz Museum and he offered me a little — a few shows of my own. So I interviewed Hymie Shertzer and then I interviewed Ray Nance when I was about 15 or so. And I said some of the stupidest things. I have a cassette of it somewhere, just horrible. You’ll never hear them. But the bottom line was so already this interest in history — so I met Benny Goodman at that exhibit thing when I was 15, and around the same time, when we were going to hear Teddy Wilson play with my parents, Teddy was playing at a place called the Cookery, which was at 9th Street and University Place, which was owned by Barney Josephson, who used to own Café Society. And then in the early 70s he had Alberta Hunter made her comeback at this club, and Teddy Wilson played there, and all kinds of people. Well my parents took me down to see Teddy Wilson one night, this is all happening in these years. And Teddy had a tuxedo on, and the date, I’m not one of those date people but I happen to remember it because I can picture it, it’s either 1972 or ’73. I think it was ’72. And Teddy is dressed in a tuxedo which he never wore. I said, “Oh Mr. Wilson, why are you wearing a tuxedo.” He said well they’re giving a — the National Urban League is giving an award to Lionel Hampton tonight at the Waldorf, and I’m going from here to there, and we’re re-uniting the original Benny Goodman Quartet will be playing. And I couldn’t believe it. You © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

know I said oh my God, you know. He went, “Well would you like to come with me.” “Would I like to come with you?” But then how am I going to — my father is going to have to drive back and leave me for three or four hours and then either go back to Fairlawn or go sit somewhere, and I went with Teddy Wilson and I got autographs. It was Lionel Hampton, Gene Krupa, Benny Goodman, Lionel Hampton, Illinois Jacquet played with them, and I think it was George Duvivier or Slam Stewart. And I got all these autographs. And that was the first time that I met Goodman and then when he came to the Jazz Museum I said well I had got your autograph, as though he would remember you know. And he said well maybe you want to come — and I wanted an autographed picture. He said, “Well call my office.” So I called his office and it was on a weekend or something, I went in and it was a woman named Muriel Zuckerman, who had been Benny Goodman’s personal aide for 40 years, like a real Girl Friday kind of thing. She was in love with the boss and a wonderful woman. And I went in and I got this autograph of Benny Goodman, little did I know that I would be running that office several years later. So this is all just giving context to what happened to me before I went to college. Then also in New Jersey there was a jazz workshop at a place called Ramapo College. And it was one of the first I think serious like jazz like summer jazz workshop kind of thing for kids. This was in the early 70s, mid 70s. And it was run by a man named Harold Lieberman, a wonderful trumpet player. He did some studio work. And he had an assistant working for him by the name of Dick Lowenthal. And so they had this wonderful program. And among the faculty were Frankie Dunlop, the drummer who played with Thelonious Monk, Bucky Pizzarelli, Derek Smith, and oh man there was someone else who I just am blanking on, Paul Jeffrey, the saxophone player. And Kenny Washington, I met him there, he was on this thing. And so I was very lucky, when I said about luck, you know because at that time kind of like a burgeoning of jazz education for kids, the Jazz Museum happened to start in New York, Teddy Wilson happened to have a weekend off from playing in Hackensack, New Jersey, and all these things are just coming together. Well I fell in love with the Benny Goodman record at Carnegie Hall, and for whatever reason I zeroed in on this tenor sax solo that Lester Young played on that concert. And I had taken a couple of clarinet lessons, never got very far on it, but at least I learned the fingering. And there was a tenor sax in the high school band room. And I kind of taught myself to play it. I mean it’s not hard to teach yourself the saxophone if you’ve taken a couple of clarinet lessons. I mean it’s very simple fingering and much simpler than the clarinet.
Yes, more friendly.
And so I picked it up and slowly began this move towards not focusing exclusively on the piano but starting to play the saxophone. So that all happened at that time. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
At 15 years of age.

About 15 or so. Yeah. And one last thing that was probably a real key component of all these things in terms of getting into school and becoming more professional was that at the Jazz Museum one of Jack Bradley’s closest friends was the cornetist Ruby Braff. And Ruby was a real character and I eventually became his personal manager and that’s another story. But Ruby heard me play the piano at the museum, as much as I could play, and he kind of said you know it’s pretty bad he says, but you know you’ve got some potential there. You really should study with this guy named Sanford Gold, who was kind of a legendary — well I didn’t know — kind of a legendary piano teacher in New York in the 60s, 70s, maybe 50s, 60s, 70s, and all kinds of people studied with him from A to Z classical, jazz, he taught technique but he also married the study of the piano into theory. So as you learned — I mean he didn’t teach beginning players but as you learned to play this Chopin etude or as you learned to play “Waltz for Debby” or whatever it was, you were mapping out the harmonic sphere. And he had his own system of diminished chords and substitution chords and all this kind of stuff. It was pretty good. And so I studied with — so what happened was he charged $25 a lesson. This was 1973 or so. And that was unheard of. I mean I was taking piano lessons in Ridgewood, New Jersey for, I don’t know, for $5 or $10. And my parents were really skeptical. And one day when my dad came to pick me up at the Jazz Museum Ruby came out with Jack Bradley and they talked to my father. My dad didn’t know who Ruby Braff was except that Jack probably said he’s a great musician. He said, “Mr. Schoenberg, you know, your son has some talent but he’s really not too good but if he has any potential he should go with Sanford Gold, it’s $25.” And he said, “I’m sorry but we can’t, we’re not going to do that.” And Ruby and Jack said, “Well we’ll pay for it then.” Now whether they really would have or not I don’t know, it doesn’t make a difference. But the gesture of having said that convinced my parents that I should study with Sanford Gold and that is probably the most significant thing that happened to me in between playing the piano at four years old and getting into Manhattan School of Music as a piano minor, third year piano minor when I was 17 or 18. Because Sanford Gold could hear wrong fingering. He could hear wrong fingering. And it’s not just me saying it, he was famous for it. He’d be in another part of the room facing another way while you were playing, and he’d say, “Second finger.” I mean he could tell from the articulation of the note. Now also studying with him at that time were Jon Faddis and Lew Soloff, who were both new in New York and roommates I guess, or very close friends, and they were studying with him. They couldn’t have been, I mean Jon is not that much older than me, he was probably 19 or something. And I remember they were crazy and I remember meeting other people in those days at his © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
studio. So if you put all that together it starts to give you a picture of where I was when I went to college.
You went to college before you went to college.
Yes. You know that’s a good —
That’s the way I feel about it. Because you can’t pay for that stuff that you got.

Absolutely. A question you asked a while ago was like did I realize or did I know like you mentioned you were in a car with Milt Hinton over here asleep on your shoulder. You’re saying now wait a minute, this is not just some old bass player, this is Milton J. Hinton and this is Fiddler Claude Williams or these people. And the only way to answer your question is you know you were older when that happened to you, I assume you were in your 30s or something.
Yes.

For me in my teens frankly I thought that’s the way the life was. And I mean I treated them with great respect. Of course I think now about how I behaved and I go oh my God. But no I mean I had no idea of how great it was.
Yeah. In some ways it’s great. I mean when I was in my teens I had a couple of experiences but they were a different level, like Chuck and Gap Mangione in Rochester.
Oh. Yeah.

Okay? So that was my thing. And at the time it was the same. I was respectful, I was a little envious, they’re doing what I would like to do. But and then later on when you know the history of these people. So that’s a heck of a story. Jazz has been called America’s only original art form.
When you transcribe this you can transcribe that I’m going to roll my eyes.
Okay. Well I’m rolling mine too and I’m off camera.
He’s off camera, okay.
But what about the blues?
What about the blues?
What about the blues? Isn’t the blues its own original American art form?
Yeah. I guess so, yeah.
Okay. Why did you roll your eyes?

Because there’s two things that I roll my eyes at, and I roll them in great respect. I mean, and he did roll his eyes, that those kind of statements I don’t know how much good they do. I don’t know how much light they shed on anything, because well what about cartoons? What about a certain kind of cinema? What about any number of things that are uniquely American. I mean early on Albert Murray had me read a book called American Humor by Constance Rourke, it was written back around 1930 or so. segments.title: Opening: archive notices and introduction of Loren Schoenberg
segments.summary: Copyright notice, biographical note and Monk Rowe's introduction.

segments.title: Deciding on music: supportive parents and Manhattan School of Music plans
segments.summary: Schoenberg says music felt pre-ordained, describes his New Jersey high school band director and acceptance at Manhattan School of Music in 1976, and his parents' support.

segments.title: Al Jolson records, old movies and falling for Benny Goodman
segments.summary: His father's Jolson 78 started him; he collected, watched old films and found Goodman's 1938 Carnegie Hall album at the library. He also reflects on minstrelsy and race.

segments.title: Piano lessons, Teddy Wilson in Hackensack and parents meeting musicians
segments.summary: Early piano lessons, then seeing Teddy Wilson at a Hackensack restaurant; his parents befriend Wilson, Hank Jones and Eddie Durham and trust them as mentors.

segments.title: Sociology versus musicology in teaching jazz history
segments.summary: Schoenberg says jazz development is sociology; his course starts with colonial New Orleans, and he credits Albert Murray and Stanley Crouch.

segments.title: Jazz Education Network convention and the state of jazz
segments.summary: He reflects on the Reno convention, jazz education and teaching today's kids, and calls himself very lucky.

segments.title: Awareness of significance: Hank Jones and starting at the New York Jazz Museum
segments.summary: Answering Rowe's Milt Hinton story, he recalls Hank Jones driving him home and volunteering at the New York Jazz Museum in 1972 under Jack Bradley.

segments.title: Museum visitors and the Basie exhibit opening with Mingus on bass
segments.summary: Weekend volunteering, people like Marge Singleton and Harry Carney, and recording the Basie exhibit opening where Mingus took the bass.

segments.title: Threading films, meeting Dan Morgenstern and corresponding with Russ Connor
segments.summary: Running film shows at the museum, meeting Dan Morgenstern, and writing to Goodman discographer Russ Connor.

segments.title: Goodman exhibit, Hymie Shertzer, radio shows and Teddy Wilson at the Cookery
segments.summary: Meeting Hymie Shertzer, doing WBAI radio interviews, and going with Teddy Wilson to the Goodman Quartet reunion at the Waldorf.

segments.title: Meeting Goodman, Ramapo workshop and teaching himself tenor sax
segments.summary: Getting Goodman's autograph, the Ramapo jazz workshop faculty, and self-teaching tenor from a Lester Young solo.

segments.title: Studying with Sanford Gold, paid for by Ruby Braff
segments.summary: Ruby Braff urges lessons with Sanford Gold; Braff and Bradley offer to pay, and Gold's gift for hearing fingerings.

segments.title: College before college: teenage awareness of the greats
segments.summary: Schoenberg says as a teen he thought mentors like Hinton were normal life; Rowe shares his own Mangione experience.

segments.title: Eye-rolling at 'America's only art form' and 'classical music'
segments.summary: He objects to the clichés that jazz is America's only original art form, its classical music, or once its popular music.

segments.title: Whether musicians were conscious of their place in history
segments.summary: Rowe suggests players don't think of history; Schoenberg names those who did.

segments.title: Explaining jazz to people who say they don't get it
segments.summary: The salmon analogy: people feel compelled to say they know nothing about jazz, which he calls stigmatization.

segments.title: Race, minstrelsy and taking jazz into the concert hall
segments.summary: Why jazz became stigmatized: nineteenth-century lies, minstrelsy, and removing the music from social settings.

segments.title: Musicians' responsibility to the audience; saving Part Two
segments.summary: Musicians' exclusivity and failure to explain; they agree to revisit in Part Two.

segments.chapter: Manhattan School of Music and Eddie Durham
segments.title: Manhattan School of Music and Phil Schaap's West End Cafe
segments.summary: Entering MSM in 1976, studying with Joe Allard, and Phil Schaap's seven-night jazz scene at the West End.

segments.chapter: Manhattan School of Music and Eddie Durham
segments.title: Sitting in with Francis Williams and Eddie Durham; Goshen gig
segments.summary: He sits in with Williams and Durham, then plays in Durham's quartet in Goshen, NY for years.

segments.chapter: Manhattan School of Music and Eddie Durham
segments.title: Warmth of older Black musicians and music as life
segments.summary: Being welcomed as a young Jewish kid by older Black musicians; music comes out of life; link to teaching context.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
segments.title: Goodman calls: cataloguing his library for the New York Public Library
segments.summary: Goodman calls in his fourth year of college to document his library for the New York Public Library; Schoenberg leaves school.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
segments.title: Leaving school for Goodman, freelancing, and the 1979 Bird and Prez tribute concert
segments.summary: Playing in many bands, then the 1979 concert tribute with Howard McGhee, Dickie Wells and others.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
segments.title: Bob January's band and starting a rehearsal big band
segments.summary: Led Bob January's stock band, then formed his own rehearsal band with Mel Lewis and others.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
segments.title: Becoming Goodman's personal manager; John Hammond and Buck Clayton
segments.summary: Goodman's assistant quits, he becomes his manager, while his band gets gigs and charts, and John Hammond brings Buck Clayton.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
segments.title: Recording 'That's The Way It Goes' and Goodman's silent reaction
segments.summary: The 1984 record's personnel and RCA session, and Goodman playing it in the background without comment; chauffeuring him.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
segments.title: Goodman hires the band for the 1985 anniversary and fires Schoenberg
segments.summary: Goodman refuses a reunion band for PBS, hires Schoenberg's band, then replaces him with Ted Nash.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
segments.title: After Goodman: no ghost band, MusicMasters albums
segments.summary: After Goodman's death he declined a ghost band and recorded albums using Moscow-tour commissions.

segments.chapter: American Jazz Orchestra, conducting and teaching
segments.title: American Jazz Orchestra with John Lewis
segments.summary: The AJO at Cooper Union, its personnel, Central City Sketches with Benny Carter and Ellington recordings.

segments.chapter: American Jazz Orchestra, conducting and teaching
segments.title: Conducting in Cologne, Smithsonian Jazz Orchestra, Ellington scores, New School start
segments.summary: Conducting the WDR orchestra, substituting for the Smithsonian orchestra, transcribing Ellington scores, and starting at the New School.

segments.chapter: American Jazz Orchestra, conducting and teaching
segments.title: New School classes, Manhattan School teaching, WBGO and Sirius radio
segments.summary: Teaching, radio at WBGO, and Kenny Washington's Sirius programming.

segments.title: Becoming Bobby Short's musical director
segments.summary: Schoenberg lists his teaching and radio jobs, then in 1997 becomes Bobby Short's musical director after a joke about a big band.

segments.title: Short's hotel gig, forming the Carlyle band and the Street of Dreams arrangement
segments.summary: A one-off hotel gig leads to a ten-week Carlyle run; his esoteric Street of Dreams arrangement flopped due to seating; other arrangers took over.

segments.title: Bobby Short as orchestrator-pianist; meeting Len Garment
segments.summary: Short's gift for Strayhorn-like orchestration and counterpoint; a thousand shows, and Teddy Wilson's thumb remark.

segments.title: Len Garment and the failed first jazz museum
segments.summary: Garment's Nixon arts career and the first national jazz museum project dying.

segments.title: Founding the Jazz Museum in Harlem with Garment's million dollars
segments.summary: Opening offices in 2001-02, restricted federal funding, board members Marsalis and Burns, Appelbaum design.

segments.title: Public oral histories and programs
segments.summary: Public programming and oral histories became the museum's identity, including lesser-known people.

segments.title: Harlem in the Himalayas at the Rubin Museum; museum growth
segments.summary: The Rubin Museum concert series, a Kenny Davern story, and hiring staff with Batiste and McBride.

segments.title: New building and collections
segments.summary: The move to a new building and collections including Ellison's records and Lockjaw Davis's saxophone.

segments.title: Praise for the Fillius archive and an offer to swap interviews
segments.summary: Schoenberg praises Rowe's archive and proposes interviewing Rowe in return.

segments.title: Closing and thanks
segments.summary: They agree on a plan and say goodbye.
